english: Really? — a polite check that you heard right, mild surprise or interest.
usage: polite -요, to anyone you'd use 존댓말 with
casual banmal, to a friend or younger person
fuller polite form, slightly stronger doubt
natural extension asking about a situation
examples: A: 나 합격했어 / B: 정말?!
A: I passed / B: Really?!
the bare one-word reaction in banmal — quick mild surprise between friends
A: 이거 무료예요 / B: 정말요? 감사합니다!
A: This is free / B: Really? Thank you!
polite 정말요 to a staff member giving good news — safe and natural in any service context
A: 사장님이 오늘 일찍 보내준대 / B: 정말요? 웬일이래.
A: The boss says he'll let us off early / B: Really? What's gotten into him.
workplace situation: surprised but pleased reaction; 정말요 stays polite toward a coworker while 웬일이래 adds humor
nuance: 정말요? (polite) / 정말? (casual) is the everyday 'really?' you say to confirm you heard correctly — it signals mild surprise or interest, not strong disbelief. Literally 정말 'truly' + polite particle -요, so dropping -요 flips it to banmal immediately: use plain 정말? only with friends or those younger than you, and keep 정말요? with bosses, elders, or any stranger. The nearest alternative is 진짜요?, but the dividing line is register feel: 정말요? is the neutral, safe choice that even works in formal contexts, while 진짜요? is warmer and more colloquial. As a variation, 정말이에요? pushes a bit harder, implying you want to verify the claim — not just a reflex. The classic English-speaker trap is intonation: 정말요 MUST rise sharply to read as a question; said flat it becomes the adverb 'truly' (정말 감사합니다 'I'm truly grateful') and the listener waits for you to finish. Also, don't stack 정말 진짜요? — that's redundant; pick one.

structuredNuance.t: 정말요? is the everyday 'really?' you say to confirm you heard right — mild surprise or interest, NOT strong disbelief. It works at any politeness level by toggling the -요 suffix.

Plain 정말? is banmal — to friends or younger people. With a boss, elder, or any stranger you must keep the -요: 정말요?. Even in formal or semi-formal settings 정말요? holds up; 진짜요? can feel a touch too casual there.

진짜요? and 정말요? overlap as 'really?' but 진짜요? is warmer and more spontaneous — the default among friends. 정말요? is more neutral and registers as safer in formal or unfamiliar settings. 정말이에요? is a fuller form that implies you want to double-check a claim, not just react.
Core forms: 정말? (banmal) → 정말요? (polite) → 정말이에요? (fuller doubt) → 정말 그래요? (asking about a situation). Stronger disbelief uses 말도 안 돼요 instead.
Intonation: 정말요 said FLAT sounds like the adverb 'truly,' not a question — the pitch must rise at the end. Also, never stack 정말 진짜요? ('really really?'); Koreans use one, not both.

mistakes: Saying plain 정말? to a boss or elder — the bare form is banmal and too casual; keep the polite 정말요? with anyone you use 존댓말 with.
Saying it flat without rising intonation — 정말 with no upward pitch reads as the adverb 'truly,' not the question 'really?'; the pitch must rise.
Stacking 정말 진짜요? to sound more surprised — these are two words for the same thing; native speakers use one, not both together.

english: Really?! / for real? — surprised, more colloquial and emotional than 정말요.
usage: polite -요, casual-friendly tone with strangers your age
casual banmal, very common among friends
examples: A: 나 로또 됐어 / B: 진짜?!
A: I won the lottery / B: For real?!
the bare banmal reaction — excited, can't-believe-it surprise between friends
A: 그 식당 오늘 문 닫았어요 / B: 진짜요? 아쉽다.
A: That restaurant is closed today / B: Really? What a shame.
polite-casual 진짜요 to a coworker; natural in everyday office small talk
A: 우리 팀 이겼대! / B: 진짜? 대박, 언제?
A: They say our team won! / B: For real? Awesome, when?
real situation: 진짜 flows straight into 대박 in excited casual chat — this is a very natural chain
nuance: 진짜요? (polite) / 진짜? (casual) is the more emotional, colloquial cousin of 정말요? — it leaks genuine excitement and surprise in a way 정말요? doesn't. Literally 진짜 'real/genuine' (the 진 is the Sino-Korean 眞 'true') + polite -요; 진짜? alone is banmal. The dividing line against 정말요? is tone and setting: 진짜? is the default 'really?' among friends because it's warm and spontaneous, while 정말요? is more neutral and holds up in stiffer formal contexts where 진짜요? can feel a touch too relaxed. The key variant ladder is 진짜? (bare casual) → 진짜요? (polite-ish) → 진짜예요? (fuller, doubting) → 진짜 진짜? (doubling for playful disbelief). The English-speaker pitfall is register over-confidence: 진짜요? has -요 but still carries an informal flavor — with a CEO or in ceremony, the cleaner choice is 정말요?. Also, like 정말요?, intonation must rise; said flat 진짜 becomes the emphasis adverb 'genuinely' (진짜 좋아 'I genuinely like it') rather than a question.

structuredNuance.t: 진짜요? is the more emotional, colloquial 'really?!' — it leaks genuine surprise and excitement. 진짜? alone is banmal; add -요 for a polite-ish but still informal version.
진짜 comes from Sino-Korean 眞짜 — 眞 (진) meaning 'true/genuine.' So 진짜 is literally 'the real thing,' and 진짜? means 'is this the real thing?' i.e., 'for real?'

진짜? is the default casual 'really?' among friends because it's warmer and more spontaneous. 정말요? is safer in formal or unfamiliar settings. In stiff contexts (a CEO, a ceremony), 정말요? is cleaner. 정말요? and 진짜요? are not always interchangeable in feel.
진짜? (banmal) → 진짜요? (polite-casual) → 진짜예요? (fuller doubt) → 진짜 진짜? (playful disbelief doubling).

Register over-confidence: 진짜요? has -요 but its flavor is still casual — with a CEO or in ceremony, use 정말요? instead. Intonation must rise; said flat, 진짜 becomes the emphasis adverb 'genuinely,' not the question 'for real?'

mistakes: Using 진짜요? in a very formal or ceremonial setting — it stays casual in flavor; with a CEO or in a formal context use 정말요? or 그래요?.
Saying flat 진짜 expecting it to mean 'really?' — without rising pitch it's the emphasis adverb 'for real / genuinely,' a statement, not a question.
Confusing 진짜 (real, the opposite of fake) with 정말 in writing — as a reaction they overlap, but 진짜 is more colloquial and 정말 more neutral; don't assume they're interchangeable in every sentence.

english: Awesome! / wow / no way — a big reaction to something amazing, shocking, or extreme.
usage: casual banmal, to friends, very common
examples: A: 나 승진했어 / B: 대박!
A: I got promoted / B: Awesome!
the bare slang reaction between friends — pure excited celebration
A: 이 카페 디저트 봐 / B: 와, 대박이다.
A: Look at this cafe's dessert / B: Wow, that's amazing.
everyday: reacting to something visually impressive; 와 대박이다 is a very natural chain
A: 옆집에 불났대 / B: 헐, 대박. 다친 사람은 없대?
A: They say the next building caught fire / B: Whoa, no way. Anyone hurt?
real situation: 대박 reacts to shocking bad news too — the follow-up question shows 대박 doesn't mean it's good
nuance: 대박 literally means 'a big hit / jackpot' (대 大 'big' + 박 = jackpot), and as a reaction it explodes out for anything extreme — amazingly good, but also shocking or unbelievably bad. It is youth slang and firmly casual: 대박 alone is banmal among friends; for even a little politeness say 대박이에요, though that still reads as informal in flavor. The variant ladder is 대박 → 대박이다 → 대박이에요 → 완전 대박 (intensified). The dividing line against 헐 is emotional direction: 헐 leans toward shock/dismay ('oh no, whoa'), while 대박 leans toward 'wow, that's enormous' — though both can appear together as 헐 대박. Because it's casual slang, the English-speaker pitfall is using it in formal or hierarchical settings — to a boss or elder, 대박 sounds flippant and disrespectful; use 대단하네요 or 굉장하네요 instead. A second pitfall is assuming it's always positive: Koreans say 대박 at a car crash too, meaning 'unbelievable/shocking.'

structuredNuance.t: 대박 literally means 'big jackpot/hit.' As a reaction it explodes out for anything extreme: something amazingly good, surprising, or even shockingly bad. The literal origin is the lucky strike in a bet or harvest — now stretched into a general 'wow' for anything over-the-top.

대박 is casual youth slang — banmal by default. Use with friends and peers. With a boss or elder it sounds flippant and disrespectful; switch to 대단하네요 or 굉장하네요. Even 대박이에요 (polite form) retains an informal, youthful flavor.

대박 is 'wow, this is huge!' — the emphasis is scale and amazement. 헐 leans toward shock/dismay ('oh no, what?!'). They often appear together as 헐 대박 when something is both shocking and enormous. 대박 can be positive or negative; 헐 skews negative.
대박 (banmal bare) → 대박이다 (casual exclamatory) → 대박이에요 (polite) → 완전 대박 (intensified). Note: 대박요 is unnatural — the noun needs 이에요, not raw -요.

Using 대박 with a boss or in formal settings — it's youth slang and sounds rude there. Also, assuming it's only positive: 대박 reacts to anything extreme, including shocking bad news. Adding 대박요 is unnatural; the polite form is 대박이에요.

mistakes: Using 대박 with a boss, professor, or elder — it's casual slang and sounds disrespectful in formal settings; use 대단하네요 or 굉장하네요.
Assuming 대박 is only for good news — it reacts to anything extreme, including shocking bad events; tone and context decide the meaning.
Adding -요 as 대박요 — that's not natural; the polite form is 대박이에요, since 대박 is a noun that needs the 이에요 copula.

english: Whoa / OMG / no way — a gut reaction of shock, disbelief, or mild dismay.
usage: casual banmal, friends and texting, very common
paired with 대박 for double shock
shock plus asking if it's true
oh no, what do we do
examples: A: 나 폰 잃어버렸어 / B: 헐.
A: I lost my phone / B: Whoa.
the bare interjection — instant shock between friends; one syllable, immediate
A: 시험이 내일이래 / B: 헐, 나 하나도 공부 안 했는데.
A: They say the exam is tomorrow / B: OMG, I haven't studied at all.
everyday: 헐 opens the reaction, then you explain your distress — very natural texting chain
A: 걔네 헤어졌대 / B: 헐, 진짜? 왜?
A: They say those two broke up / B: Whoa, really? Why?
real situation: 헐 is the gut reaction; 진짜? asks for confirmation; 왜? asks for detail — a classic three-step gossip chain
nuance: 헐 is a pure interjection of shock — the involuntary sound that comes out when something startling, dismaying, or unbelievable hits you. It's hugely common in texting and casual conversation among friends and younger people. Because it's a raw exclamation there is no polite form: there is no 헐요 or 헐이에요; it lives entirely in banmal territory. The dividing line against 대박 is emotional direction: 헐 carries surprise often tinged with 'oh no' or dismay, while 대박 leans toward 'wow, that's enormous' — that's why 헐 어떡해 (shock + worry) is a natural pair but 대박 어떡해 is odd. Also don't confuse 헐 with 헉: 헐 is drawn-out disbelief ('whoa, no way'), while 헉 is a sharp one-syllable gasp of fright or physical surprise. The English-speaker pitfall is using 헐 in a professional or respectful setting — to an elder or boss it sounds childish and rude; in those moments use 어머 for neutral surprise or a full 정말요? 그런 일이. A second pitfall is trying to write 헐요 to be polite — simply switch words.

structuredNuance.t: 헐 is a pure interjection of shock — the involuntary sound you make when something startling, dismaying, or unbelievable hits you. It is hugely common in texting and casual speech. It lives entirely in banmal/casual territory; there is no polite version of 헐 itself.

Strictly casual — among friends and peers, in texts and informal chat. To an elder or boss it sounds childish and rude. In formal or respectful situations, react with 어머 (neutral gasp) or 정말요? 그런 일이 (full polite expression of shock). There is no 헐요 — just switch words.

헐 skews toward shock and dismay ('oh no, whoa'). 대박 skews toward 'wow, enormous.' They often pair as 헐 대박 for maximum shock. 헉 is a short gasp of fright or physical surprise — more sudden and bodily, while 헐 is drawn-out disbelief.
헐 alone is most common. Common expansions: 헐 대박, 헐 진짜?, 헐 어떡해 (shock + worry). You can write multiple 헐헐헐 in texts to show escalating disbelief.

Using 헐 with a boss, elder, or in a formal context — it sounds immature and rude there. Trying to add -요 as 헐요 — that form doesn't exist; switch to 어머 or 정말요? instead. Mixing up 헐 (drawn-out disbelief) with 헉 (sharp fright gasp).

mistakes: Using 헐 with a boss, elder, or in a formal email — it's casual youth slang and sounds immature/rude; use 어머 or 정말요? instead.
Trying to make a polite version like 헐요 — it doesn't exist; 헐 is a raw interjection that stays casual, so switch words for politeness.
Mixing up 헐 and 헉 — 헐 is disbelief/dismay ('whoa, no way'), while 헉 is a startled gasp of fright; they aren't interchangeable.

english: Wow, that's cool / awesome — admiring something or someone impressive.
usage: with 진짜 to intensify the praise
examples: A: 나 마라톤 완주했어 / B: 와 멋있다!
A: I finished the marathon / B: Wow, that's awesome!
the bare admiring reaction — praising a friend's achievement
A: 이 야경 좀 봐 / B: 와, 멋있다.
A: Look at this night view / B: Wow, that's gorgeous.
everyday: admiring a beautiful sight; 멋있다 naturally covers impressive scenery, not just people
A: 부장님이 영어로 발표하셨어 / B: 와, 멋있으시다. 정말 대단하세요.
A: The manager presented in English / B: Wow, that's so impressive. You're really remarkable.
real situation: honorific 멋있으시다 + 대단하세요 when praising a senior — stacking compliments is natural here
nuance: 와 멋있다 is the spontaneous 'wow, that's cool/awesome/impressive' you exclaim at something or someone admirable. 와 is the gasp 'wow' and 멋있다 means 'is cool/stylish/admirable.' The plain 멋있다 is the casual exclamatory form used even to oneself, 멋있어요 is polite, and when praising a senior you insert honorific -으시-: 멋있으시다 or 멋있으세요. The variant ladder is 멋있다 → 멋있어요 → 멋있으시다 → 진짜 멋있다 (intensified). The dividing line against 예쁘다 and 대단하다 is the type of admiration: 멋있다 is cool/stylish/admirable (a skill, a view, an attitude), 예쁘다 is cute/pretty (appearance, small charming things), 대단하다 is remarkable/impressive in terms of effort or achievement. A hiker who summited alone → 멋있다 AND 대단하다 both work, but 멋있다 adds a cooler, more stylish tone. The English-speaker pitfall is avoiding the exclamatory -다 ending because it looks like a dictionary base form — but 멋있다! as a live reaction is completely natural spoken Korean. Another pitfall is praising a senior with plain 멋있어 and omitting the honorific -으시-.

structuredNuance.t: 와 멋있다 is the spontaneous 'wow, that's cool/awesome' you exclaim at something or someone impressive. 와 is the gasp 'wow'; 멋있다 means 'is cool/stylish/admirable.'

Plain 멋있다 is casual and used to oneself or friends. Polite: 멋있어요. Honorific for elders/seniors: 멋있으시다 / 멋있으세요. Add 진짜/완전 before 멋있다 to intensify. Never use plain 멋있어 with a senior — it sounds over-familiar.

멋있다 = cool/stylish/admirable (a skill, a scene, an attitude). 예쁘다 = cute/pretty (looks, small charming things). 대단하다 = remarkable/impressive for effort or achievement. A drone pilot's skill → 멋있다; their hard years of practice → 대단하다; a flower arrangement → 예쁘다.

Avoiding 멋있다! as a live reaction because -다 looks like dictionary form — but bare -다 exclamations are completely natural spoken Korean. Praising a senior with plain 멋있어 / 멋있다 instead of honorific 멋있으세요 / 멋있으시다 — that sounds too familiar.

mistakes: Praising a boss or elder with plain 멋있어 / 멋있다 — for a senior add honorific -으시-: 멋있으세요 / 멋있으시다, or you sound too familiar.
Using 멋있다 for something cute or pretty — that's 예쁘다; 멋있다 is for cool/stylish/admirable things, a different flavor of praise.
Avoiding 멋있다! as a reaction because -다 looks like dictionary form — the bare -다 exclamation is natural spoken Korean for live admiration.

english: That's great / good for you / it worked out — happy something turned out well.
usage: that's great / glad it worked out
with 정말 to warm up the congratulation
examples: A: 나 그 회사 붙었어 / B: 잘됐다!
A: I got into that company / B: That's great!
the bare reaction — sharing a friend's good news; 잘됐다 expresses happiness for them, not yourself
A: 엄마 수술 잘 끝났어 / B: 아, 정말 잘됐다. 걱정했잖아.
A: Mom's surgery went well / B: Oh, I'm so glad. I was worried.
everyday: 잘됐다 + acknowledgment of prior worry — shows you genuinely cared; 정말 warms it further
A: 비자 드디어 나왔어요 / B: 잘됐어요! 고생 많으셨어요.
A: My visa finally came through / B: That's wonderful! You worked so hard for it.
real situation: polite 잘됐어요 plus 고생 많으셨어요 acknowledges the effort behind the result — a natural pairing
nuance: 잘됐다 means 'it turned out well / that's great' — the warm, celebratory reaction when a good outcome arrives. Built from 잘 'well' + 되다 'to turn out, to happen,' frozen as an exclamation: 잘됐다/잘됐어 (casual), 잘됐어요 (polite), 잘됐네(요) (softly reacting to news). The key dividing line versus 다행이다 is the emotional starting point: 잘됐다 is happy at good news with no prior dread attached — 'yay, it worked out!'; 다행이다 implies you were worried and disaster was dodged — 'thank goodness, what a relief.' A job offer you hoped for → 잘됐다; a health scare that turned out fine → 다행이다. A second near-synonym is 다행히 잘됐다, which blends both feelings. The English-speaker pitfall is the spelling/spacing: it must be written as one word 잘됐다 (not 잘 됐다 with a space, not 잘 됬다 — 됬다 is always wrong; the past of 되다 is 됐다). Another critical pitfall is tone: if you say 잘됐다 flat or with a sarcastic lilt it flips to 'serves you right,' so keep your voice clearly warm.

structuredNuance.t: 잘됐다 literally means 'it went well / turned out well.' As a reaction it means 'that's great / I'm so happy for you.' It's not just an observation — it carries emotional warmth and shared happiness.
잘됐다/잘됐어 are casual banmal. 잘됐어요 is polite and safe with coworkers, seniors, or clients. 잘됐네요 softly reacts to news heard in the moment. To warm it up further, prepend 정말 or 너무.

잘됐다 = happy at good news, no prior worry needed. 다행이다 = relieved because a feared bad outcome didn't happen — the worry is the key component. A passed exam where you studied confidently → 잘됐다. A passed exam you feared failing → 다행이다.

Spelling: write 잘됐다 as one word (not 잘 됐다 or 잘 됬다). 됬다 is always wrong — the past of 되다 is 됐다 (되+었=됐). Tone trap: said flatly or with a sarcastic edge, 잘됐다 means 'serves you right.' Keep your voice warm to show it's sincere.

mistakes: Writing 잘됬다 — this spelling is always wrong; the past of 되다 is 됐다 (되+었), so it's 잘됐다.
Using 잘됐다 when you mean 'what a relief' — for a feared outcome that didn't happen use 다행이다; 잘됐다 is for genuinely good news.
Saying 잘됐다 flatly or with a sour tone — it can flip to sarcastic 'serves you right'; keep your voice warm so it reads as sincere congratulations.

english: Thank goodness / what a relief — relieved that something bad was avoided.
usage: casual with -네 on hearing reassuring news
examples: A: 검사 결과 괜찮대 / B: 다행이다.
A: The test results are fine / B: Thank goodness.
the bare reaction — pure relief exhaled; the context of earlier worry makes 다행이다 feel right here
A: 지갑 택시에서 찾았어 / B: 아, 다행이다. 걱정했잖아.
A: I found my wallet in the taxi / B: Oh, what a relief. I was so worried.
everyday: 다행이다 + 걱정했잖아 ('I was worried') — this pairing is very natural and shows the worry-then-relief arc
A: 사고 났는데 다친 데는 없어요 / B: 다행이에요, 정말. 몸조심하세요.
A: There was an accident but no one's hurt / B: That's such a relief, truly. Please take care.
real situation: polite 다행이에요 reacting to a serious near-miss with a senior; 정말 intensifies; 몸조심하세요 is the natural follow-up
nuance: 다행이다 is the 'thank goodness, what a relief' you breathe out when a feared bad outcome was avoided — built from the noun 다행 'good fortune (that it wasn't worse)' + the copula 이다. The variant ladder is 다행이다/다행이야 (casual) → 다행이에요 (polite) → 다행이네(요) (softly on hearing news) → 천만다행이다 (for a grave near-miss, '천만 = ten million' times lucky). The critical dividing line versus 잘됐다 is the emotional starting point: 다행이다 implies you were worried and disaster was dodged; 잘됐다 is happiness at good news with no prior dread. Surgery that ended safely → 다행이다; a job offer you hoped for → 잘됐다. The English-speaker pitfall is translating 'lucky' as 운이 좋다 — that means fortunate in a winning-the-raffle sense, while 'what a relief it wasn't bad' is specifically 다행이다. Another pitfall is dropping the copula and saying just 다행 — that's a noun left incomplete; native speakers always say 다행이다 or 다행이에요 to close the sentence.

structuredNuance.t: 다행이다 is the exhaled 'thank goodness / what a relief' when a feared bad outcome was avoided. The emotional arc is: worry → something could have gone wrong → it didn't → relief. Without that prior worry, the natural word is 잘됐다, not 다행이다.

다행 is a Sino-Korean noun (多幸 — 多 'many/much' + 幸 'good fortune/blessing') meaning 'good fortune, fortunate outcome.' Adding copula 이다 makes it a complete reaction. 천만다행 (千萬多幸) means '10 million blessings' — hyperbole for an enormous relief.

다행이다 = you were worried and it turned out okay (relief from fear). 잘됐다 = it turned out well, happy news (no fear required). 운이 좋다 = you were lucky/fortunate in a positive-outcome sense (winning a raffle). A near-miss accident with no injuries → 다행이다, NOT 잘됐다 or 운이 좋다.
다행이다/다행이야 (casual) → 다행이에요 (polite) → 다행이네요 (reacting to news) → 천만다행이다 (serious near-miss). Never drop the copula: 다행 alone is an incomplete sentence.

Translating 'lucky' as 운이 좋다 when you mean relief — 운이 좋다 is fortuitous luck, not relief from fear. Saying 다행 alone without the copula — it's a noun and needs 이다/이에요. Using 다행이다 for joyful good news when no worry was involved — that's 잘됐다.

mistakes: Saying 다행 by itself — it's a noun and needs the copula: 다행이다 (casual) or 다행이에요 (polite) to be a complete sentence.
Using 운이 좋다 ('lucky') for relief — 운이 좋다 means fortunate/got a break, but 'phew, it wasn't bad' is 다행이다, a different feeling.
Swapping in 잘됐다 — 잘됐다 is happiness at good news, while 다행이다 specifically means a feared bad outcome was avoided; the worry is the key difference.

english: What do I do? / oh no — distressed, not knowing how to handle a problem.
usage: what do I do? / oh no
what do I do / oh no
fuller form, asking for a real solution
examples: A: 마지막 버스 끊겼어 / B: 어떡해.
A: The last bus is gone / B: Oh no.
the bare reaction between friends — dismay at a problem; here it's a pure exclamation, not asking for advice
A: 발표 자료를 안 가져왔어요 / B: 어떡해요, 지금 출력 가능해요?
A: I didn't bring the presentation file / B: Oh no, can you print it now?
everyday: 어떡해요 as polite dismay that naturally pivots to problem-solving in the same breath
A: 너 핸드폰 액정 깨졌어 / B: 헐, 어떡해, 이거 산 지 일주일 됐는데.
A: Your phone screen is cracked / B: OMG, oh no, I only bought it a week ago.
real situation: 어떡해 as pure distress, not a literal request for instructions — the rhetorical use is very common
nuance: 어떡해(요) is the distressed 'oh no, what do I do?!' that bursts out when a problem hits and you feel stuck or overwhelmed — it is often a pure emotional exclamation, not a literal request for instructions. It's the contracted spoken form of 어떻게 해 'how (shall I) do (this)': casual 어떡해, polite 어떡해요. Said softly toward someone else's misfortune it also means sympathetic 'oh no, poor you.' Variants: 나 어떡해 (with subject, stressing your own predicament), 어떡하지 (casual, slightly milder, pondering aloud). The critical dividing line is spelling: 어떡해 is the emotional contraction you exclaim, while 어떻게 is the adverb 'how' that modifies another verb (어떻게 가요? 'how do I get there?') — they are not interchangeable. The English-speaker pitfall is writing 어떻해 (a non-word combining both forms) or using 어떻게 where the exclamation 어떡해 belongs. Register-wise, 어떡해 is banmal, so to a boss or elder use 어떡해요; to actually ask for a solution use 어떻게 하면 좋을까요?.

structuredNuance.t: 어떡해 is a contraction of 어떻게 해 — literally 'how (should I) do (it)?'. But as a live reaction it's usually not asking for instructions. It's an emotional exclamation of dismay: 'oh no / what do I do?!' The actual meaning is 'I'm overwhelmed by this problem,' not 'please give me a plan.'

어떡해 is casual banmal. With a boss or elder use 어떡해요. To genuinely ask for a solution (not just exclaim) say 어떻게 하면 좋을까요? (polite) or 어떻게 해? (casual). When comforting someone else about their trouble, 어떡해 or 어떡해요 works as sympathetic 'oh no, poor you.'
chips: 해결 방법 요청 → 어떻게 하면 좋을까요?

structuredNuance.t: 어떡해 = emotional exclamation of dismay ('oh no!'). 어떻게 = adverb 'how,' always modifying a verb (어떻게 해요? 어떻게 가요?). 어떡하지 = casual, pondering-aloud version of 어떡해 — slightly softer, wondering what to do rather than exclaiming. These are not interchangeable.

Writing 어떻해 — not a word; the exclamation is 어떡해 (contraction) and the adverb is 어떻게 (never combined). Using 어떻게 as an exclamation of dismay — 어떻게 alone is just 'how?' and sounds unfinished. Saying plain 어떡해 to a boss or elder — keep the -요 or switch to a full polite phrase.

mistakes: Writing 어떻해 — this is not a word; the exclamation is 어떡해 (contraction of 어떻게 해), and the adverb is 어떻게.
Using 어떻게 where you mean the dismay 'oh no' — 어떻게 is 'how' (어떻게 해요? = how do I do it), while the panicked exclamation is 어떡해(요).
Saying plain 어떡해 to a boss or elder — it's banmal; use 어떡해요, or to ask for actual help say 어떻게 하면 좋을까요?.

english: That's a shame / too bad / I wish it were different — mild regret or disappointment.
usage: casual with -네 reacting in the moment
it's a bit of a letdown
with 좀 to soften it further
examples: A: 표 다 팔렸대 / B: 아쉽다.
A: The tickets are all sold out / B: That's a shame.
the bare reaction — light disappointment; 아쉽다 is exactly right for a small letdown, not 슬프다
A: 저 다음 주에 이사 가요 / B: 아, 아쉬워요. 자주 봤는데.
A: I'm moving next week / B: Oh, that's too bad. We saw each other so often.
everyday: polite 아쉬워요 expressing regret at parting; the follow-up 자주 봤는데 explains WHY it's a shame
A: 비 와서 소풍 취소됐어 / B: 아쉽다. 날씨만 좋았어도.
A: The picnic got canceled because of rain / B: What a shame. If only the weather had held.
real situation: 아쉽다 paired with a wistful -았/었어도 conditional ('if only X') — this is a very natural 아쉽다 follow-up pattern
nuance: 아쉽다 is mild, wistful regret — 'that's a shame / I wish it were otherwise' — the feeling when something nice didn't happen, ended too soon, or fell just short. It's soft; it's NOT deep sadness. The variant ladder: 아쉽다/아쉬워 (casual) → 아쉬워요 (polite) → 아쉽네(요) (in-the-moment reaction to news) → 좀 아쉽다 (softened, noting a small lack). Note the conjugation: 아쉽다 is a -ㅂ irregular adjective, so the polite stem is 아쉬워요 (아쉽+어요 → 아쉬워요), never 아쉽어요. The dividing line against 슬프다 and 속상하다: 아쉽다 is a gentle 'aw, too bad' about a missed chance or something pleasant ending; 슬프다 is real sadness (loss, grief); 속상하다 is being genuinely hurt or upset inside (frustration, heartache). Sold-out tickets → 아쉽다; a pet dying → 슬프다; your work criticized unfairly → 속상하다. 아쉽다 also covers the sense of 'feeling a lack / something's missing' (뭔가 아쉽다 'something feels lacking'), so context decides. The English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 슬프다 for everyday letdowns — to a Korean ear that's melodramatic.

structuredNuance.t: 아쉽다 is mild, wistful regret — 'that's a shame / I wish it were otherwise.' It covers both 'disappointed a nice thing didn't happen' and 'feeling a small lack.' It is NOT deep sadness; it's a gentle sigh.
아쉽다/아쉬워 (casual) → 아쉬워요 (polite) → 아쉽네(요) (in-the-moment reaction). 좀 아쉽다 softens it further. Conjugation note: -ㅂ irregular, so polite = 아쉬워요, NOT 아쉽어요.

아쉽다 = mild regret / missed chance (gentle). 슬프다 = real sadness/grief (deep emotion). 속상하다 = hurt/upset inside (frustrated or heartbroken). 아깝다 = 'what a waste' (something valuable was wasted or lost). Sold-out tickets → 아쉽다; a pet dying → 슬프다; unfair criticism → 속상하다; spilling expensive wine → 아깝다.

Using 슬프다 for small everyday disappointments — to a Korean ear that's melodramatic; 아쉽다 is the right word. Conjugating as 아쉽어요 (wrong; -ㅂ irregular makes it 아쉬워요). Confusing 아쉽다 with 아깝다 — 아깝다 is about wasted value, 아쉽다 is about a missed wish.

mistakes: Using 슬프다 ('sad') for small letdowns like a canceled plan — that sounds melodramatic; the natural word for mild regret is 아쉽다.
Confusing 아쉽다 with 아깝다 — 아깝다 is 'what a waste / too good to waste' (about value/resources), while 아쉽다 is 'a shame, wish it were otherwise' (about a missed chance).
Conjugating the -ㅂ irregular adjective wrong: the polite form is 아쉬워요 (아쉽+어요 → 아쉬워요), not 아쉽어요.

english: I'm upset / it hurts / it's distressing — genuinely bothered or heartsick about something.
usage: that must be so upsetting for you
examples: A: 키우던 화분이 다 죽었어 / B: 아, 속상하겠다.
A: All my plants died / B: Oh, that must be so upsetting.
the empathy reaction — using -겠- to guess the other's feeling, NOT saying 속상해요 which would sound like you yourself are upset
A: 열심히 했는데 결과가 안 좋아서 속상해요.
A: I worked hard but the result was bad, so I'm really upset.
everyday: politely expressing your own inner hurt after effort that didn't pay off — the earnestness in 열심히 했는데 makes 속상해요 resonate
A: 애가 말을 안 들어서 너무 속상해요 / B: 속상하시겠어요. 힘드시죠.
A: My kid won't listen, I'm so upset / B: That must be so upsetting. It must be hard.
real situation: honorific 속상하시겠어요 + 힘드시죠 to comfort an elder — the -시- honorific in both clauses shows full respect
nuance: 속상하다 literally means 'the insides (속) are hurt/spoiled (상하다)' — a vivid metaphor for the gnawing, heartsick feeling when something genuinely bothers, frustrates, or grieves you inside. Casual 속상해, polite 속상해요, honorific empathy 속상하시겠어요 'that must hurt for you.' The dividing line against 화나다 is direction: 속상하다 is inward hurt/distress (you're sad-frustrated, maybe near tears), while 화나다 is outward anger directed at someone. Your child ignoring you → 속상하다 (heartache); a rude stranger → 화나다 (anger). They can co-exist: 화나고 속상해요 'I'm both angry and hurt.' The empathy structure is key: to comfort someone, Koreans use -겠- to infer the other's feeling — 속상하겠다 / 속상하시겠어요 ('that must be upsetting for you'). Saying just 속상해요 about someone else's situation sounds like you are the one upset, not them. The English-speaker pitfall is translating 'upset' as 화나다 — English 'upset' typically covers both hurt-sad and angry; in Korean these split into 속상하다 (hurt inside) and 화나다 (outward anger).

structuredNuance.t: 속상하다 literally means '속 (insides) are 상하다 (spoiled/hurt)' — a vivid body metaphor. In use it means a deep inner distress: being hurt, frustrated, and a little heartbroken simultaneously. It's heavier than 아쉽다 and specifically about something that gnaws at you inside.

속상해 (casual banmal to friends) → 속상해요 (polite) → 속상하시겠어요 (honorific empathy for a senior). For expressing another person's probable feeling use -겠-: 속상하겠다 / 속상하시겠어요. Conjugation note: 하다 → 해요, NOT 하요.

속상하다 = inward hurt/distress (sad + frustrated, often near tears). 화나다 = outward anger directed at someone. 슬프다 = sadness/grief (loss, not necessarily involving another person's fault). They can combine: 화나고 속상해요. Child ignoring you → 속상하다; rude stranger → 화나다; pet's death → 슬프다.

Translating English 'upset' as 화나다 — English 'upset' covers both hurt and angry, but Korean splits them: inward hurt = 속상하다, outward anger = 화나다. Using 속상해요 to empathize with someone else — you need -겠- to infer their feeling: 속상하겠어요 / 속상하시겠어요. Conjugating as 속상하요 (wrong — should be 속상해요).

mistakes: Translating English 'upset' as 화나다 — 화나다 is outward anger; hurt/distressed 'upset' is 속상하다, an inward feeling.
Comforting someone with 속상해요 instead of 속상하겠어요 — to guess another person's feeling use -겠-: 속상하겠다 / 속상하시겠어요 ('that must be upsetting for you').
Conjugating it as 속상하요 — it's an adjective in 하다, so the polite form is 속상해요 (하 + 여 → 해), not 속상하요.

english: Ugh, so annoying / this is irritating — frustration at something getting on your nerves.
usage: casual banmal, venting to a friend
polite -요, but still informal in flavor
examples: A: 또 에러야 / B: 아, 짜증 나.
A: It's an error again / B: Ugh, so annoying.
the bare vent between friends — low-grade prickly frustration, not deep anger
A: 버스 또 놓쳤어. 진짜 짜증 나.
A: Missed the bus again. So annoying.
everyday: venting a small daily frustration to yourself or a friend; 진짜 before 짜증 나 intensifies it naturally
A: 옆에서 계속 시끄럽게 해서 짜증 났어 / B: 아, 그럴 만하다.
A: They kept being loud next to me, it got on my nerves / B: Yeah, that's understandable.
real situation: 짜증 나다 in past tense (짜증 났어) describing something that irritated you over time; 그럴 만하다 is a natural empathic reply
nuance: 짜증 나 means 'it's irritating / getting on my nerves' — the low-grade, prickly frustration of small annoyances piling up (repeated errors, delays, noise). 짜증 is the noun 'irritation/peevishness' and 나다 means 'arises,' so literally 'irritation arises.' The particle structure is 짜증(이) 나다 — 짜증 is the subject that 'comes up,' which means 짜증해 (treating it as a 하다 verb) is not a real form. Casual 짜증 나; exclamatory 짜증 난다; polite 짜증 나요 exists but still sounds blunt. Related: 짜증 내다 means 'to show/express irritation' (you actively let it out). The dividing line against 화나다 is degree and direction: 짜증 나다 is low-grade, diffuse annoyance ('ugh, this again'), while 화나다 is real anger directed at someone. The English-speaker pitfall is the verb form: don't say 짜증해 or 짜증을 해 — the correct forms are 짜증(이) 나다 (it arises) or 짜증 내다 (you express it). Another pitfall is register: even 짜증 나요 carries a raw, blunt edge, so to an elder or boss soften to 좀 힘드네요 or 불편하네요.

structuredNuance.t: 짜증 나 is literally 'irritation arises' — 짜증 (noun: irritation/peevishness) + 나다 (to arise). The real meaning is the prickly, low-grade frustration of small things getting on your nerves. It's NOT deep anger — it's the 'ugh, again?!' feeling.

짜증 나 is casual banmal — for venting to friends or peers. 짜증 나요 is polite but still blunt in flavor — fine with coworkers your age but avoid with elders or bosses. With seniors, soften to 좀 힘드네요 (a bit tough), 불편하네요 (a bit uncomfortable), or 어렵네요 (it's difficult).

짜증 나다 = irritation arises (passive; something is getting on your nerves). 화나다 = anger arises at someone (stronger, directed outward). 짜증 내다 = you actively EXPRESS or show your irritation (can annoy others around you). 짜증 나다 + 화가 나다 can co-occur when something both annoys and angers.

Saying 짜증해 or 짜증을 해 — there's no verb 짜증하다; it's 짜증(이) 나다 (irritation arises) or 짜증 내다 (to show irritation). Using 짜증 나요 with a boss or elder — even with -요 it's too raw; use 좀 힘드네요 or 불편하네요. Confusing 짜증 나다 with 화나다 — the first is low-grade diffuse annoyance, the second is real anger at someone.

mistakes: Saying 짜증해 or 짜증을 해 — there's no verb 짜증하다; it's 짜증(이) 나다 (irritation arises) or 짜증 내다 (to show irritation).
Using 짜증 나요 with a boss or elder — even the -요 form is raw/blunt; soften to 좀 힘드네요 / 불편하네요 in respectful settings.
Confusing 짜증 나다 with 화나다 — 짜증 나다 is low-grade peevish annoyance, while 화나다 is genuine anger at someone; they differ in intensity.

english: I'm so excited / this is fun / yay — bubbling, happy excitement.
usage: casual exclamatory, to oneself or friends
with 완전 to amp up the excitement
examples: A: 내일 여행 가! / B: 신난다!
A: We go on the trip tomorrow! / B: Yay!
the bare reaction — bubbling joy at something coming; exclamatory -다 form is natural here
A: 오늘 일찍 끝나서 신나.
A: We finish early today, so I'm excited.
everyday: casual self-expression of happy excitement; 신나 as a plain statement to a friend
A: 콘서트 티켓 구했어! / B: 진짜? 신난다! 빨리 가고 싶다.
A: I got the concert tickets! / B: Really? Yay! I can't wait to go.
real situation: 신난다 + 빨리 가고 싶다 is a very natural chain — the excitement immediately becomes eager anticipation
nuance: 신난다 is bright, bubbling excitement — 'yay, this is so fun / I can't wait!' — the happy energy buzz before or during something enjoyable. Built from 신(이) 나다 'spirit/mood arises': plain 신나 (casual), exclamatory 신난다, polite 신나요. Because it's cheerful and casual, it's perfect among friends but too breezy for formal settings. The variant ladder: 신나 → 신난다 → 완전 신난다 (hyped). The dividing line against 기대돼요 and 재미있다: 신나다 is active, energetic excitement right now (you're bouncing); 기대되다 is calm, forward-looking anticipation ('I'm looking forward to it'); 재미있다 describes how fun an activity actually IS or WAS (not about anticipation). Road-trip vibe the night before → 신난다; quietly looking forward to seeing an old friend → 기대돼요; describing how the trip turned out → 재미있었어. The English-speaker pitfall is using 흥분되다 for 'excited' — 흥분되다 means agitated/worked-up (can imply arousal or anger) and sounds very off for innocent fun; the right word for happy excitement is 신나다. A second pitfall is expressing enthusiasm to a superior with 신난다 — it's too casual; use 기대돼요 or 정말 기쁩니다.

structuredNuance.t: 신난다 comes from 신(이) 나다 — 신 (spirit/energy/mood) + 나다 (to arise). Literally 'the spirit arises.' As a reaction it means 'I'm buzzing with excitement / yay!' — active, energetic, happy anticipation.
신나 (casual plain) → 신난다 (casual exclamatory) → 신나요 (polite but informal-flavored). 완전 신난다 intensifies. With a superior or in a formal setting, switch to 기대돼요 or 정말 기쁩니다 — 신난다 sounds too breezy.

신나다 = active, energetic excitement right now (you're bouncing with enthusiasm). 기대되다 = calm forward-looking anticipation ('I'm looking forward to it'). 재미있다 = describes how fun an activity IS or WAS (assessment). Trip-eve energy → 신난다; quietly anticipating → 기대돼요; recounting how fun it was → 재미있었어.

Using 흥분되다 for 'excited' — 흥분되다 means agitated/worked-up (can imply arousal or even anger) and sounds jarring for innocent fun. The right word for happy excitement is 신나다. Using 신난다 with a boss or superior — it's casual; switch to 기대돼요 or 정말 기쁩니다.

mistakes: Translating 'excited' as 흥분되다 — that means agitated/worked-up (can imply arousal or anger); cheerful excitement is 신나다.
Saying 신난다 to a boss to show enthusiasm — it's breezy and casual; in respectful settings use 기대돼요 or 정말 기쁩니다.
Forming it as 신하다 or 신해 — there's no such verb; it's 신(이) 나다, so the forms are 신나 / 신난다 / 신나요.

english: Whoa, you scared me! / yikes — startled when something jumps out or surprises you suddenly.
usage: with 아 as the natural gasp lead-in
examples: (친구가 갑자기 등장) A: 야! / B: 아, 깜짝이야!
(friend pops up suddenly) A: Hey! / B: Oh, you scared me!
the bare startle — instant reflex; 아 leads in naturally before 깜짝이야
A: 뒤에서 갑자기 부르지 마, 깜짝이야.
A: Don't call me from behind suddenly, you scared me.
everyday: mild complaint after being startled — 깜짝이야 at the end explains WHY the request is being made
A: (문 열다 마주침) 어머! / B: 아, 깜짝 놀랐어요. 안에 계신 줄 몰랐어요.
A: (opens door, bumps into someone) Oh! / B: Oh, you startled me. I didn't know you were inside.
real situation: polite 깜짝 놀랐어요 to a senior after a mutual startle — you can't use 깜짝이야 politely, so you switch to 깜짝 놀랐어요
nuance: 깜짝이야 is the reflex 'whoa, you scared me!' that bursts out the instant something startles you — a friend appearing suddenly, a loud noise, a jump-scare. It comes from 깜짝 (the mimetic/sound-symbolic word for a sudden flinch) + 이야 (casual 이다 declaration). Because it's a raw reflex exclamation it's inherently casual; there's no polite 깜짝이에요 that sounds natural. In a respectful situation you switch to 깜짝 놀랐어요 ('I was startled') which carries the same meaning with -어요 politeness. The dividing line against 무섭다 ('I'm scared/afraid') is duration: 깜짝이야 / 깜짝 놀라다 is a momentary jolt that's over in a second, while 무섭다 is sustained fear or dread (a horror movie, a threatening person). A friend jumping out → 깜짝이야; a dark alley at night → 무서워. The English-speaker pitfall is saying 너 나를 무섭게 했어 ('you scared me' — literal translation) — that's unnatural; Koreans say 깜짝 놀랐잖아 or 깜짝이야. Another pitfall is treating 놀라다 as transitive: you can't 'scare someone' directly with 놀라다 — the person 놀라다 (gets startled); to say you startled them use 놀라게 하다.

structuredNuance.t: 깜짝이야 is built from 깜짝 — a mimetic (sound-symbolic) word for a sudden flinch or start — + 이야 (casual copula). Literally 'it's a 깜짝!' meaning 'what a shock!' As a reaction it means 'you startled me / you scared me!' — an instant, involuntary exclamation.

깜짝이야 is casual/banmal — a raw reflex that you can't really dress up. With a senior or in a formal situation, switch to 깜짝 놀랐어요 ('I was startled') to convey the same meaning politely. 아, 깜짝이야 with the lead-in 아 is the most natural everyday form.

깜짝이야 / 깜짝 놀라다 = momentary jolt of surprise (over in a second). 무섭다 = sustained fear/dread (horror movie, threatening situation). 헉 = a sharp gasp of fright, slightly more physical than 깜짝이야. Friend jumping out → 깜짝이야; dark alley → 무서워; sudden loud bang → 헉.

Saying 너 나 무섭게 했어 for 'you scared me' — that's a literal but unnatural calque; Koreans say 깜짝 놀랐잖아 or 깜짝이야. Treating 놀라다 as transitive: 놀라다 is intransitive (the person gets startled); to say you caused it use 놀라게 하다. Using 무섭다 for a momentary startle — 무섭다 is sustained fear, not a flinch.

mistakes: Saying 너 나 무섭게 했어 for 'you scared me' — that's a literal, unnatural calque; natives say 깜짝 놀랐잖아 or 아, 깜짝이야.
Using 무섭다 for a momentary startle — 무섭다 is sustained fear/dread; a sudden jolt of surprise is 깜짝 놀라다 / 깜짝이야.
Treating 놀라다 as 'to scare (someone)' — the person 놀라다 (is startled); to startle them you say 놀라게 하다, since 놀라다 itself is intransitive.

english: No way / that's ridiculous / unbelievable — strong disbelief at something absurd or shocking.
examples: A: 그 사람이 1등이래 / B: 말도 안 돼.
A: They say that person came first / B: No way.
the bare reaction — flat, strong disbelief; 말도 안 돼 rejects the claim as impossible, not just 'really?'
A: 집값이 두 배 올랐대 / B: 말도 안 돼. 어떻게 그래?
A: They say housing prices doubled / B: That's ridiculous. How is that even possible?
everyday: disbelief at outrageous news; 어떻게 그래? is a natural follow-up to extend the protest
A: 환불이 안 된다고 하시네요 / B: 네? 말도 안 돼요. 영수증도 있는데요.
A: They're saying no refunds / B: What? That's outrageous. I even have the receipt.
real situation: polite 말도 안 돼요 protesting something unfair — with -요 it's still firm but directed appropriately at a service situation
nuance: 말도 안 돼 literally means 'it doesn't even become words' → 'that makes no sense / no way / this is ridiculous' — a strong reaction of disbelief or protest at something absurd, shocking, or unfair. Built from 말+도 안 되다 — 말 'words/speech,' 도 'even (additive particle),' 안 되다 'doesn't work out.' (Note: the subject particle 이 is dropped when 도 follows: 말이+도 → 말도.) Casual 말도 안 돼, polite 말도 안 돼요. The dividing line against 진짜? / 정말요? is strength: 진짜? is a light 'really?' that is open to it being true; 말도 안 돼 flatly rejects the claim as impossible or outrageous — much stronger. It also differs from 대박 ('wow, huge'): 대박 can be amazed positive or shocked; 말도 안 돼 specifically protests/rejects. The English-speaker pitfall is the spelling: 돼 is 되+어, never just 되; writing 말도 안 되 (without the final ㅓ vowel) is a very common error. Another pitfall is register/strength — 말도 안 돼요 to a superior can sound confrontational; to push back politely use 그럴 리가요 ('surely not') or 이해가 안 되네요 ('I don't quite understand').

structuredNuance.t: 말도 안 돼 literally means 'it doesn't even become words' — the idea is so absurd or wrong that language itself can't accommodate it. In use: strong disbelief, rejection, or protest at something ridiculous or unfair. It is NOT just 'really?' — it actively denies the claim.

말도 안 돼 is casual banmal. 말도 안 돼요 is polite. Both are strong in tone, so with a superior or in a polite dispute you may need to soften further: 그럴 리가요 ('surely not'), 이해가 안 되네요 ('that doesn't quite make sense to me'). 말도 안 돼요 to a boss in anger can sound confrontational.

진짜? = light 'really?' — open-minded, you might believe it. 말도 안 돼 = strong rejection — you flatly disbelieve or protest it. 그럴 리가(요) = polite/softer disbelief ('it can't be / surely not') — same rejection, but gentler register, safer with seniors.

Spelling: 돼 = 되+어, NOT just 되; writing 말도 안 되 as a sentence-final reaction is a common error. Treating it like mild surprise — it's strong; for a light 'really?' use 진짜? or 정말요?. Using it confrontationally with a superior — soften to 그럴 리가요 or 이해가 안 되네요.

mistakes: Writing 말도 안 되 — the form is 말도 안 돼 (되+어 = 돼); as a sentence-final reaction it must end in 돼, not 되.
Using 말도 안 돼(요) for mild surprise — it's strong rejection ('impossible/ridiculous'); for open-minded 'really?' use 진짜? / 정말요?.
Dropping 말도 안 돼요 on a superior in a dispute — it can sound confrontational; to push back politely use 그럴 리가요 or 이해가 안 되네요.

english: Right? / exactly / I know, right — agreeing that you feel the same, often a bit helplessly.
usage: polite -요, agreeing with someone you respect
yeah, right / tell me about it
examples: A: 오늘 진짜 덥다 / B: 그러게.
A: It's really hot today / B: Right?
the bare agreement — echoing a shared feeling; you feel it too, so 그러게 is exactly right here
A: 요즘 왜 이렇게 시간이 빨라요 / B: 그러게요, 벌써 6월이에요.
A: Why does time fly these days / B: I know, right — it's June already.
everyday: polite agreement with a mutual observation; the 벌써 6월이에요 follow-up adds your own evidence of the shared feeling
A: 그때 그거 샀어야 했는데 / B: 그러게 말이에요. 지금은 품절이래요.
A: We should've bought it back then / B: Exactly. It's sold out now apparently.
real situation: 그러게 말이에요 agreeing with a shared regret — the emphatic form feels more heartfelt than bare 그러게요
nuance: 그러게(요) means 'right? / exactly / I know, I feel the same' — you agree with something the other person said, often with a faint helpless, resigned, or rueful tinge. It's built from 그러다 'to be/do like that' + the sentence-final 게/게요. Casual 그러게, polite 그러게요, emphatic 그러게 말이에요 'exactly, you said it.' The critical dividing line is against 그렇구나 / 그렇군요: 그러게(요) responds to a SHARED feeling or opinion you already hold ('I know, right'), while 그렇구나 / 그렇군요 reacts to NEW information you just learned ('oh, I see / I didn't know that'). Both respond to something the other person just said, but the agreement type is opposite. Saying 그러게요 to new facts implies you already knew and can sound dismissive. To a superior 그러게요 is acceptable but 맞아요 / 그러네요 can feel a touch more attentive and engaged. The English-speaker pitfall is using 그러게요 as a response to new information — e.g., someone tells you their hometown for the first time and you say 그러게요, which would mean 'I know' and imply you already knew. The second pitfall is misreading its tone as disagreement; it is agreement, just with a resigned or rueful undertone.

structuredNuance.t: 그러게(요) means 'right? / I know / exactly' — you agree with something the other person just said, often with a faint resigned or rueful undertone ('yeah, I know, what can you do'). It is agreement, not disagreement.

그러게 (casual banmal to friends) → 그러게요 (polite, to seniors/coworkers) → 그러게 말이에요 (emphatic full agreement) → 그러게 말이야 (casual emphatic, half-resigned). With a superior, 맞아요 or 그러네요 can feel slightly more attentive.

그러게(요) = 'I know, right' — confirms shared feeling/opinion you already held. 그렇구나 / 그렇군요 = 'oh, I see' — reacts to NEW information you just learned. 맞아요 = 'that's right / correct' — cleaner factual agreement, less rueful. Swap 그러게요 for 그렇군요 with new info or you sound like you already knew.

Using 그러게요 to react to brand-new information — that implies you already knew and sounds dismissive. Misreading 그러게요 as doubt or disagreement — it is definitely agreement. Saying plain 그러게 to a boss or elder — banmal; use 그러게요 or 그러게 말이에요.

mistakes: Using 그러게요 to react to brand-new information — that implies you already knew; for news you just learned use 그렇군요 / 그렇구나.
Saying plain 그러게 to a boss or elder — it's banmal; keep the polite 그러게요 (or 그러게 말이에요) with anyone you use 존댓말 with.
Reading 그러게요 as disagreement or doubt — it actually means 'right, I feel the same,' a soft, often resigned agreement.

english: Oh my / oh! — a quick gasp of surprise, more neutral and usable than 헐.
usage: neutral surprise, common (esp. women, all ages)
oh my, what do we do
examples: A: (컵을 떨어뜨림) / B: 어머!
A: (drops a cup) / B: Oh!
the bare gasp — instant surprise at a sudden event; pure reflex
A: 이거 선물이에요 / B: 어머, 뭘 이런 걸 다. 감사해요.
A: This is a gift for you / B: Oh my, you shouldn't have. Thank you.
everyday: pleased-surprised reaction to a gift; 뭘 이런 걸 다 ('you didn't have to') is the perfect polite follow-up after 어머
A: 비 갑자기 쏟아진다 / B: 어머, 우산도 없는데 어떡해.
A: It's suddenly pouring / B: Oh my, and I don't have an umbrella, what do I do.
real situation: 어머 triggers 어떡해 as surprise flows naturally into worry — this two-step chain is very common in women's speech
nuance: 어머 is a quick, soft gasp of surprise — 'oh!' / 'oh my' — far more neutral and polite-safe than slangy 헐 or 대박. It is a pure interjection so it doesn't take -요; to be polite you follow it with a full polite sentence. The register difference: 어머 is gentle, refined surprise that anyone can use across ages and contexts, including in front of elders and in semi-formal moments where 헐 would sound rude. Stronger and more emphatic is 어머나; surprise that turns to worry naturally extends as 어머 어떡해. A social note: 어머 / 어머나 is used by everyone but has a stronger association with women's speech; men tend to reach for 어 / 어이쿠 / 헐 instead. The dividing line against 헐: 헐 is casual youth slang with a shock/dismay tilt, while 어머 is softer and registers as more composed and socially graceful. The English-speaker pitfall is defaulting to 헐 in every surprised moment — with an older Korean or in a slightly formal context, 헐 can sound rude, so 어머 is the safe default. Another pitfall is treating 어머 as filler and saying it flatly; it carries genuine emotional color and should sound like a real gasp.

structuredNuance.t: 어머 is a soft gasp of surprise — 'oh!' / 'oh my' — neutral and polite-safe across ages and contexts. It's a reflexive interjection (no -요 attached); politeness comes from the full sentence that follows.

어머 works in casual AND semi-formal settings — safe with elders, colleagues, or strangers where 헐 would sound rude. It doesn't take -요 directly. Social note: commonly used by women of all ages; men often prefer 어 / 어이쿠. 어머나 is stronger; 어머 어떡해 adds worry.

헐 = casual youth slang, shock/dismay tilt — only among friends and peers; sounds rude with elders. 어머 = softer, more refined surprise, cross-generational, polite-safe. 어이쿠 = similar neutral gasp, slightly more physical surprise (oops/ow/yikes), skewing male speech. All three are interjections that don't take -요.
어머 (base gasp) → 어머나 (stronger emphasis) → 어머 어떡해 (surprise + worry). In texts you might write 어머나 세상에 for dramatic emphasis. None of these take a -요 suffix directly.

Defaulting to 헐 in every surprised moment — with elders or in formal contexts 헐 is rude; 어머 is the neutral, graceful default. Adding -요 as 어머요 — interjections don't take -요; follow 어머 with a full polite sentence instead. Saying 어머 flatly without genuine surprise energy — it carries real emotional color and should sound like a true gasp.

mistakes: Defaulting to 헐 in every surprised moment, including with elders — 헐 is slang and can sound rude; 어머 is the neutral, polite-safe gasp.
Adding -요 as 어머요 — it's a reflexive interjection and doesn't take -요; for politeness, follow it with a full polite sentence.
Treating 어머 as meaningless filler — it carries genuine surprise/emotion, so saying it flatly with no feeling sounds odd; it should sound like a real gasp.

english: I see / so that's how it is — calmly taking in information you've just been told.
usage: I see / ah, so that's how it is
polite -요, composed acknowledgment of new info; slightly formal in feel
casual banmal, to a friend or someone younger; warmer and more natural in chat
the 아 marks the moment it lands — sounds more engaged than a bare 그렇군요
honorific -시- inserted when the new information is about the listener themselves
examples: A: 이 건물은 주말엔 문을 닫아요 / B: 아, 그렇군요. 몰랐어요.
A: This building closes on weekends / B: Ah, I see. I didn't know.
the core use — a fact you learned this second; 몰랐어요 makes explicit that it's new to you
A: 제가 원래 부산 사람이에요 / B: 그러시군요. 어쩐지 사투리가 살짝 들리더라고요.
A: I'm originally from Busan / B: Oh, I see. That's why I could hear a bit of the dialect.
info about the listener → honorific 그러시군요; the follow-up shows you actually did something with what you heard
A: 그래서 예약을 다시 잡아야 해요 / B: 그렇군요. 그럼 언제가 괜찮으세요?
A: So we have to rebook the appointment / B: I see. Then when works for you?
workplace/service: 그렇군요 accepts the explanation without emotion and hands the turn back — neutral and composed
nuance: 그렇군요 means 'I see / ah, so that's how it is' — you are registering information you did not have a moment ago. It's 그렇다 'to be so' + -군요, the ending whose whole job is to mark a fact as newly learned; drop the -요 for casual 그렇구나/그렇군, add -시- for 그러시군요 when the news is about the listener. The dividing line against 그러게요 is the direction of the knowledge: 그러게요 says 'I know, right' about a feeling you ALREADY shared, while 그렇군요 says 'oh, I didn't know that' about something NEW — swap them and you either sound like you already knew (dismissive) or like you're learning your own opinion. Against 아 그래요?: 그렇군요 closes the loop calmly with no question attached; 아 그래요? is surprised and asks for more. Against 그렇네요: -네요 is for what you notice with your own eyes and ears (비가 오네요, looking out the window), -군요 for what you were told. The English-speaker pitfall is volume of use: textbook learners answer everything with 그렇군요 until it sounds like a distant, robotic nod. With friends 그렇구나 or 아 진짜요? sound like a person listening. Also 그렇군요 is not 알겠습니다 — that's 'understood, I'll do it,' a receipt for an instruction.

structuredNuance.t: 그렇군요 = 'I see, so that's how it is.' You are taking in information that is NEW to you, calmly and without pushing back. The -군요 ending exists precisely to flag a fact as newly learned. It is acknowledgment, not agreement and not surprise.

그렇군요 is polite and a touch composed — it fits coworkers, service situations, and anyone you use 존댓말 with. With friends it can sound stiff and distant, so use 그렇구나. When the new fact is about the listener personally (their hometown, their job, their family), add -시-: 그러시군요.

그렇군요 = NEW info, accepted calmly, no question. 그러게요 = a feeling you ALREADY shared ('I know, right') — using it on new info implies you knew all along. 아 그래요? = mild surprise that asks for more, opening the topic instead of closing it. 그렇네요 = you noticed it yourself (-네요 is for direct perception: 비가 오네요), while -군요 is for what you were told.
그렇구나 (casual) → 그렇군요 (polite) → 그러시군요 (honorific, about the listener). Prefixing 아 (아, 그렇군요) makes it sound like the fact is landing in real time rather than being ticked off a list.

Overusing it — 그렇군요 as your default reply to everything reads as flat and disengaged, a classic textbook-learner tell; vary with 그렇구나, 아 그래요?, 정말요?. Using 그렇군요 for something you already knew (that's 그러게요 or 아 맞다). Treating it as 'understood, will do' — that's 알겠습니다.

mistakes: Using 그렇군요 to respond to a shared feeling or opinion ('오늘 덥네요') — 그렇군요 frames it as news you just learned; agreeing with a feeling you also have is 그러게요 or 그러네요.
Answering every single turn with 그렇군요 — it's grammatically fine but reads as a distant, robotic nod, especially with friends; 그렇구나 or 아 그래요? sound like an actual listener.
Using 그렇군요 where 알겠습니다 is needed — a boss gives you an instruction and 그렇군요 only says 'oh, interesting,' not 'understood, I'll do it.'

english: Oh really? / is that so? — light surprise plus a nudge for the other person to tell you more.
usage: polite -요, mild surprise that invites more; requires clearly rising intonation
casual banmal, to a friend or someone younger
without the 아 it lands flatter and, with an edge, can sound like a challenge
past tense, reacting to something that already happened
examples: A: 저 그 영화 벌써 봤어요 / B: 아 그래요? 어땠어요?
A: I already saw that movie / B: Oh really? How was it?
the model pattern — light surprise, then a follow-up question; 아 그래요? alone would stall the conversation
A: 사장님 오늘 휴가세요 / B: 아 그래요? 몰랐네요.
A: The boss is on vacation today / B: Oh, is that so? I had no idea.
workplace: mild surprise at news; polite and completely safe with a coworker
A: 나 어제 너 봤는데 / B: 아 그랬어? 어디서?
A: I saw you yesterday / B: Oh yeah? Where?
casual banmal in the past tense; the reaction opens the topic rather than closing it
nuance: 아 그래요? is the everyday 'oh really? / is that so?' — you accept that what they said is true and react to it with mild surprise, then usually ask for more. The 아 is doing real work: it marks the information as landing right now, which is what makes the line sound interested rather than skeptical. Intonation is not optional here. Said with a clear rise, 아 그래요? means 'oh! tell me more.' Said flat, low, and slow, the exact same syllables become the bored 'oh, is that right' that tells your friend you'd like them to stop talking — and 그래요? without the 아, delivered with a sharp edge, tips into 'oh yeah?', a challenge. That's why beginners should keep all three parts: 아 + rise + a follow-up question. The line against 정말요?/진짜요? is what you're questioning: those ask whether the claim is TRUE (verification, mild doubt); 아 그래요? takes it as true and reacts to the news itself. Against 그렇군요: 그렇군요 absorbs the fact and closes the loop; 아 그래요? hands the turn back. And watch the punctuation — 그래요 without the rise isn't a reaction at all but agreement or consent: 그래요, 그럼 그렇게 해요 'okay, let's do that.'

structuredNuance.t: 아 그래요? = 'oh really? / is that so?' You believe what they said; you're mildly surprised by it and you want more. Its function is to keep the other person talking, which is why it almost always comes with a follow-up question (어땠어요? / 언제요? / 왜요?).

그래요? is polite and safe with coworkers, neighbors, and strangers. 그래? is the banmal partner for friends. When the news is about the listener personally and they're clearly senior to you, 아, 그러세요? / 그러시군요 sounds more deferential than a bare 그래요?.

정말요? / 진짜요? question whether it's TRUE — verification with a touch of doubt. 아 그래요? accepts it's true and reacts to the news, then asks for more. 그렇군요 also accepts it but closes the loop calmly with no question. 그러게요 agrees with a feeling you already shared — a completely different move; using it on someone's news implies you already knew.

아 그래? (casual) → 아 그래요? (polite) → 아, 그러세요? (honorific, about a senior). Past tense 아 그랬어요? / 아 그랬어? for things already finished. The 아 can be dropped, but keeping it is what makes the line sound freshly interested.

Intonation decides everything. Rising = genuine interest. Flat, low, and slow = the sarcastic-sounding 'oh, is that right,' i.e. 'I don't care' — the single most common way learners accidentally offend with this phrase. A sharp 그래요? with no 아 can read as 'oh yeah?', a challenge. And 그래요 with NO rise isn't a reaction at all — it's 'okay / sure' (그래요, 그렇게 해요).

mistakes: Saying 아 그래요? flat and low, the way English 'oh really' can be said neutrally — in Korean the falling version reads as bored or sneering; it must rise clearly to mean 'tell me more.'
Using 아 그래요? when you actually doubt the claim — for 'wait, is that TRUE?' the natural choice is 정말요? or 진짜요?; 아 그래요? already accepts what they said.
Dropping 그래요? as a standalone with nothing after it — with no follow-up question the conversation dies and you sound unmoved; pair it with 어땠어요? / 언제부터요? / 왜요?

english: Exactly / that's what I'm saying — emphatic agreement with someone's opinion or complaint.
usage: exactly / right? that's what I'm saying
polite -요, forceful agreement with an opinion
fuller polite form, stronger and more heartfelt
near-equivalent; leans even harder on 'I've been saying this'
examples: A: 요즘 배달비가 너무 비싸요 / B: 그러니까요. 음식값보다 더 나올 때도 있어요.
A: Delivery fees are so expensive these days / B: Exactly. Sometimes it comes out higher than the food.
the natural shape: you already felt this way and you pile on your own evidence
A: 회의를 굳이 금요일 6시에 잡네 / B: 그러니까. 누가 정한 거야?
A: They really scheduled the meeting for 6pm Friday / B: Right?? Who decided that?
casual banmal complaint; 그러니까 says 'you're preaching to the choir'
A: 그 길로 가면 항상 막혀요 / B: 그러니까요. 제가 진작 말씀드렸잖아요.
A: That road is always jammed / B: Exactly. I told you so ages ago, remember?
notice the edge — 그러니까요 can carry a faint 'I've been saying this all along,' fine with peers but pointed if aimed upward
nuance: 그러니까요 is emphatic agreement: 'exactly / that's what I'm saying.' It's 그러다 'to be like that' + -니까 'because,' and that etymology is why it carries a whiff of 'that's exactly WHY' — you're not just nodding along, you're endorsing their point as one you already held. The ladder runs 그러니까 (casual) → 그러니까요 (polite) → 그러니까 말이에요 (emphatic). The line against 그러게요 is intensity and posture: 그러게요 is soft and often faintly resigned, 'I know, right, what can you do'; 그러니까요 is louder and leans forward, closer to 'see? this is my point.' Against 맞아요 it's a hard grammatical line: 맞아요 confirms a FACT is correct — 서울이 수도예요 → 맞아요 — while 그러니까요 only works on an opinion, complaint, or observation. Answer a factual question with 그러니까요 and you've said nothing. It also cannot absorb new information; that's 그렇군요. The English-speaker pitfall is that 그러니까 mid-sentence is a totally different word: the connective 'so, therefore' (비가 와요, 그러니까 우산 챙기세요) and the rephrasing filler 'I mean...'. Only a standalone 그러니까(요) as a whole response is the agreement reaction. Second, aimed at a boss, that 'I've been saying this' undertone can read as pushy — 맞습니다 or 저도 그렇게 생각합니다 is safer.

structuredNuance.t: 그러니까요 = 'exactly / that's what I'm saying.' Strong agreement with an opinion, complaint, or observation the other person just made — and an implicit claim that you already thought so yourself. It leans forward; it's not a polite nod.

그러니까요 is polite and completely normal with coworkers and friends' parents. But the built-in 'as I've been saying' assertiveness means that with a boss or a much older person it can read as pushing your view. Upward, 맞습니다 / 그렇습니다 / 저도 그렇게 생각합니다 does the same job without the edge.

그러게요 = soft, often resigned 'I know, right' — sharing a feeling. 그러니까요 = emphatic 'exactly, that's my point' — endorsing a view you already held, more forceful. 맞아요 = 'that's correct' — it can confirm FACTS, which 그러니까요 cannot (a quiz answer gets 맞아요, never 그러니까요). 그렇군요 = new info you just learned, the opposite situation entirely.
그러니까 (casual) → 그러니까요 (polite) → 그러니까 말이에요 (emphatic full agreement) → 제 말이 그 말이에요 / 내 말이 (that's my point exactly). Colloquial 그니까 / 그니까요 is the same word contracted in speech and texting.

Confusing the standalone reaction with the connective: mid-sentence 그러니까 means 'so, therefore' (비가 와요, 그러니까 우산 챙기세요) or the filler 'I mean...' when you rephrase. Only 그러니까(요) as a complete response is 'exactly.' Also, using it on facts instead of opinions, and firing it at a superior, where the 'I told you so' undertone shows.

mistakes: Using 그러니까요 to agree that a fact is correct — for '서울이 한국 수도예요' the answer is 맞아요; 그러니까요 only works on an opinion, complaint, or shared observation.
Mixing up the standalone reaction with the connective 그러니까 'so/therefore' mid-sentence — 그러니까 우산 챙기세요 means 'so bring an umbrella,' not 'exactly, bring an umbrella.'
Firing 그러니까요 at a boss's remark — it carries an 'I've been saying this all along' edge that can sound like you're correcting them; use 맞습니다 or 저도 그렇게 생각합니다.

english: Oh good, that worked out — reacting on the spot to a situation turning out well.
usage: polite; -네요 = you're reacting the moment you hear it
polite, but a flat statement rather than an in-the-moment reaction
about a situation that suits everyone — not about anyone's achievement
examples: A: 다음 주에 재택근무 해도 된대요 / B: 잘됐네요! 출퇴근 시간 아끼겠어요.
A: They said I can work from home next week / B: Oh, that's great! You'll save the commute.
a situation landing well, not an achievement — 잘됐네요 fits; 축하해요 would be strange here
A: 저 3시 이후에 시간 돼요 / B: 아, 잘됐네요. 저도 그때가 편해요.
A: I'm free after 3 / B: Oh, that works out nicely. That time suits me too.
the scheduling sense — it's convenient for BOTH of you; 축하해요 is impossible in this situation
A: 아버지 검사 결과 괜찮대요 / B: 잘됐네요, 정말 다행이에요.
A: My father's test results came back fine / B: Oh good — what a relief.
paired with 다행이에요 when there was real worry: 잘됐네요 reacts to the outcome, 다행이에요 names the relief
nuance: 잘됐네요 is 잘 'well' + 되다 'to turn out' + -네요, and that -네요 is the whole point: it marks the words as a reaction forming right now, in response to news you are hearing this second, which is why 잘됐네요 sounds alive where the flatter 잘됐어요 sounds like a statement. The dividing line against 축하해요 is what produced the good outcome. 축하해요 congratulates a PERSON for something they achieved or a milestone they reached — 합격, 승진, 결혼, 졸업 — so it needs an accomplishment to attach to. 잘됐네요 only says the situation landed well, which lets it cover things nobody earned: a meeting getting canceled, two schedules matching, test results coming back clean, the rain stopping. It also works for your own convenience — 그럼 잘됐네요 'then that suits me' — something 축하해요 can never do. Flip side: for a genuine achievement, 잘됐네요 alone can land a little thin, like 'well, that worked out,' so stack them: 합격했다고요? 잘됐네요, 축하해요! Against 다행이에요, the difference is prior dread — 다행 requires that you were worried. Pitfalls: the tone trap that also haunts 잘됐다 (say it flat or clipped and it flips to a sour 'well, isn't that nice for you'), and the spelling — 됐 comes from 되+었, so 잘됬네요 is always wrong.

structuredNuance.t: 잘됐네요 = 'oh good, that worked out.' You're reacting on the spot, warmly, to a situation that turned out well. The -네요 ending is what marks it as a live reaction to news you're hearing right now, rather than a considered statement.

잘됐네요 is polite and safe with coworkers, seniors, and clients; 잘됐네 is the banmal partner for friends. For a big achievement, don't stop at 잘됐네요 — it can read as thin praise; add 축하해요 (or, if effort was involved, 고생 많으셨어요) to make it warm.

축하해요 congratulates a person for an ACHIEVEMENT or milestone (합격, 승진, 결혼) — it needs someone to credit. 잘됐네요 just says the SITUATION worked out, so it covers things nobody earned (a canceled meeting, matching schedules) and even your own convenience (그럼 잘됐네요 'then that suits me'), which 축하해요 cannot. 다행이에요 requires prior dread — relief that a feared outcome didn't happen. 잘됐어요 is the same word without the live-reaction feel of -네요.
잘됐네 (casual) → 잘됐네요 (polite, reacting to news) → 잘됐어요 (polite statement) → 그럼 잘됐네요 ('then that works out'). Prepend 정말 / 너무 to warm it up: 정말 잘됐네요.

Tone: said flat or clipped, 잘됐네요 flips to a sour 'well, isn't that nice for you' — keep your voice clearly warm. Spelling: 됐 = 되+었, so 잘됬네요 is always wrong and 잘 됐네요 with a space is off too. And using 잘됐네요 alone for someone's big win undersells it; 축하해요 belongs there.

mistakes: Reaching for 축하해요 when nobody achieved anything — for a canceled meeting or two schedules lining up, 축하해요 is nonsense; 잘됐네요 is the word for a situation that simply worked out.
Answering someone's 합격 or 승진 with only 잘됐네요 — it reads as thin, closer to 'well, that worked out'; add 축하해요 because a personal achievement needs to be credited to them.
Writing 잘됬네요 — the past of 되다 is 됐다 (되+었), so it's 잘됐네요, written as one word.

english: Me too / same here — saying that what they just said about themselves is true of you as well.
usage: polite; the ellipsis of 저도 그래요, safe with anyone you use 존댓말 with
fuller polite form — warmer and less clipped, good for feelings
a shade more formal; natural in a workplace
examples: A: 만나서 반가워요 / B: 저도요.
A: Nice to meet you / B: You too.
the classic — 저도요 stands in for 저도 반가워요; English says 'you too,' Korean says 'me too'
A: 저는 커피 안 마셔요 / B: 저도요. 카페인이 안 받아서요.
A: I don't drink coffee / B: Me neither. Caffeine doesn't agree with me.
note the negative: Korean uses the same 저도요 where English is forced to switch to 'me neither'
A: 요즘 너무 피곤해요 / B: 저도요. 잠을 제대로 못 자서요.
A: I'm so tired lately / B: Same here. I haven't been sleeping properly.
everyday empathy; adding one clause of your own keeps 저도요 from sounding like you're brushing them off
nuance: 저도요 is 저 (humble 'I') + 도 ('also') + 요 (polite tag) — an elliptical 저도 그래요 where the other person's verb is understood and dropped. That ellipsis is exactly what limits it: it only works when their sentence was about THEMSELVES and the same predicate can carry over to you. If they said something about you (칭찬해 주셔서 감사해요), 저도요 misfires and you need the verb spelled out — 저도 감사해요 or 저야말로 감사해요. One place Korean is kinder than English: 도 rides over negatives, so where English must swap 'me too' for 'me neither,' 저도요 handles both. Against 저도 그래요, the split is what kind of predicate you're echoing: 그래요 restates 'I'm like that too,' which fits states and feelings (피곤해요 → 저도 그래요 ✓) but goes vague on a specific action — A: 어제 그 카페 갔어요 → 저도요 ✓ (I went too) but 저도 그래요 ✗. 저도요 borrows their verb whatever it was; 저도 그래요 substitutes 그렇다. And 나도 is the plain banmal partner. The half-and-half 나도요 (casual 나 + polite 요) is genuinely common in speech between people on a fuzzy footing, but it's an inconsistent mix — with a boss or a stranger, say 저도요. Pitfall: it's very short, and a bare 저도요 to someone's bad news can read as making it about you.

structuredNuance.t: 저도요 = 'me too / same here.' It's an ellipsis of 저도 그래요 — the other person's verb is understood and left out. That means it only works when they said something about THEMSELVES and the same predicate can transfer to you.

저도요 is polite twice over — humble 저 plus the -요 tag — so it's safe with bosses, strangers, and elders; 나도 is the banmal partner for friends. In a formal meeting, 저도 마찬가지입니다 / 저 역시 그렇습니다 sounds more substantial than the clipped 저도요.

저도요 borrows whatever verb they used, so it covers actions too: A: 어제 그 카페 갔어요 → 저도요 ✓ ('I went too'). 저도 그래요 substitutes 그렇다 'be like that,' so it fits states and feelings (피곤해요 → 저도 그래요) but goes vague on a specific action (갔어요 → 저도 그래요 ✗). 나도 is the plain banmal version. 나도요 mixes casual 나 with polite 요 — very common in real speech between people on a fuzzy footing, but inconsistent; use 저도요 upward.
나도 (casual) → 저도요 (polite, clipped) → 저도 그래요 (polite, warmer) → 저도 마찬가지예요 / 저 역시 그렇습니다 (more formal). When you want to sound sincere rather than reflexive, spell the verb out: 저도 반가워요, 저도 피곤해요.

Using 저도요 when they said something about YOU rather than themselves — 감사해요 → 저도요 doesn't parse; say 저도 감사해요 or 저야말로 감사해요. Assuming you need a 'me neither' form for negatives — you don't, 저도요 covers both. And a bare 저도요 after someone's bad news can sound like you're redirecting to yourself; add a clause.

mistakes: Hunting for a 'me neither' equivalent after a negative sentence — Korean 도 works over negatives, so 저는 커피 안 마셔요 → 저도요 is correct; there is no separate negative form.
Replying 저도요 to something said about you, like 감사합니다 or 도와주셔서 고마워요 — the ellipsis has no verb to borrow; use 저도 감사해요 or 저야말로 감사합니다.
Saying 나도요 to a boss or a stranger because it 'has 요 in it' — 나 is casual and 요 is polite, so it's a mismatched half-form; the polite version is 저도요.

english: Oh right! — the sound of a forgotten thing suddenly surfacing in your own memory.
usage: oh right! / oh yeah, I just remembered
casual interjection; keep it as-is and continue the sentence in 해요체
the 참 stresses that it nearly slipped away
oh, now that you mention it
more composed — the safer choice in front of a boss or client
examples: A: 내일 몇 시에 만나요? / B: 아 맞다, 저 내일 병원 가야 돼요.
A: What time should we meet tomorrow? / B: Oh right — I have to go to the hospital tomorrow.
the core use: their question yanks a forgotten fact out of your own head; note 아 맞다 stays in plain form while the rest of the sentence goes polite
A: 우산 챙겼어? / B: 아 맞다! 깜빡했다.
A: Did you grab your umbrella? / B: Oh right! It totally slipped my mind.
casual banmal; 깜빡했다 'I blanked on it' is the natural partner phrase
A: 오늘 은행 문 닫아요 / B: 아 맞다, 공휴일이었죠.
A: The bank is closed today / B: Oh right, it's a holiday, isn't it.
you already knew it was a holiday and had forgotten — that's why 아 맞다 works and 그렇군요 would be wrong
nuance: 아 맞다 is the noise a memory makes when it resurfaces: 'oh right! — I forgot.' The 맞다 in it is frozen. It looks like the plain form of 맞다 'to be correct,' but as a recall interjection it never conjugates: 맞다요 doesn't exist, and 맞아요 has a different job. The dividing line is where the fact came from. 아 맞다 fires from YOUR OWN memory — you already knew this and had lost track of it; 아 그렇군요 / 아 그렇구나 fires from SOMEONE ELSE's information — the fact is new to you. Tell a Korean your birthday for the first time and get 아 맞다 back and they've just claimed they knew all along. 맞아요 / 맞네요 is a third thing again: 'you're right, that's correct,' an evaluation of their statement rather than a memory of yours. 아 그렇지 sits nearby — also self-recall, but for something logical clicking into place ('oh right, of course') rather than a forgotten errand. Register: 아 맞다 leans casual, but it's a reflex, so it passes in polite conversation as long as the sentence after it is polite (아 맞다, 저 그거 아직 안 냈어요). In front of a boss or a client, the composed 아, 그러고 보니 or 제가 깜빡했네요 reads better.

structuredNuance.t: 아 맞다 = 'oh right!' — a fact you already knew and had forgotten just resurfaced. It's about YOUR memory, not about the other person being correct. The 맞다 here is frozen as an interjection and never conjugates.

아 맞다 leans casual, but because it's a reflex it passes in polite conversation as long as what follows is polite: 아 맞다, 저 내일 못 가요. With a boss or a client, the more composed 아, 그러고 보니 or 제가 깜빡했네요 sounds better. There is no 맞다요 — don't try to build one.
chips: 상사/고객 → 아, 그러고 보니 / 제가 깜빡했네요

structuredNuance.e: VS 아 그렇군요 / 맞아요 / 아 그렇지
structuredNuance.t: 아 맞다 = the fact was already IN your head and you'd forgotten it (self-recall). 아 그렇군요 / 아 그렇구나 = the fact is NEW, coming from them — say 아 맞다 to genuinely new info and you're claiming you already knew. 맞아요 / 맞네요 = 'you're right, that's correct,' judging their statement, not recalling anything. 아 그렇지 = self-recall too, but for logic clicking into place rather than a forgotten errand.
아 맞다 (most common) → 맞다, 참 / 아 참 (stressing it nearly slipped away) → 아, 그러고 보니 (composed, safe upward) → 아, 깜빡했다 / 제가 깜빡했네요 ('it slipped my mind'), the natural follow-up.

Using 아 맞다 on brand-new information — it says 'I knew that and forgot,' so it reads as a false claim of prior knowledge; use 아 그렇군요/그렇구나. Trying to politen it as 맞다요 (doesn't exist) or 아 맞아요 (that means 'you're correct,' a different act). The fix for politeness is the sentence after it, not the interjection.

mistakes: Using 아 맞다 when someone tells you something for the first time — it means 'I knew that and forgot,' so it sounds like a false claim of prior knowledge; the right reaction to new info is 아 그렇군요 / 아 그렇구나.
Inventing a polite form 맞다요 — it doesn't exist; 아 맞다 is a frozen interjection, and you get politeness from the sentence that follows (아 맞다, 저 내일 못 가요).
Substituting 아 맞아요 for 아 맞다 with a superior, thinking it's just the polite version — 맞아요 tells them their statement is correct, which is grading them; for recall say 아, 그러고 보니 or 제가 깜빡했네요.

english: Thanks for your hard work / good work today — acknowledging the effort someone put in.
usage: polite; natural to peers and juniors — read the register note before aiming it upward
formal -습니다; the standard close of meetings and workdays
warmer and a shade more deferential than the bare form
present tense, to someone still working as you leave — never to a superior
examples: A: 오늘 회의는 여기까지 하겠습니다 / B: 네, 수고하셨습니다.
A: Let's end today's meeting here / B: Yes, thank you all for your work.
the standard workplace close, said around the room — by far the context you'll hear it in most
A: 이사 다 끝났어요 / B: 수고하셨어요. 진짜 힘드셨겠어요.
A: The move is all done / B: You worked so hard. That must have been exhausting.
to a peer after real physical labor; 힘드셨겠어요 adds the sympathy that makes it feel sincere
A: (부장님이) 다들 고생했어요 / B: 감사합니다, 부장님. 먼저 들어가 보겠습니다.
A: (The manager) Good work, everyone / B: Thank you, sir. I'll head out first.
notice the direction: the senior appraises the juniors' effort; going the other way, 감사합니다 + 먼저 들어가 보겠습니다 is the safe move
nuance: 수고하셨어요 credits someone for the effort they spent — 'thanks for your hard work.' Its natural direction is downward or sideways: a manager to the team, a colleague to a colleague, a customer to a delivery driver. Going UP the ladder it gets delicate, and the reason is worth understanding. 수고 (受苦) literally means 'to receive hardship,' and telling someone they endured hardship is an appraisal of their labor — appraising is a senior's prerogative, so a junior doing it can read as presumptuous. 국립국어원's 표준 언어 예절 states outright that 수고하셨습니다 should not be used toward 윗사람, and it puts 고생하셨습니다 in the same bucket for the same reason; what it recommends upward is 고맙습니다 / 감사합니다, or simply 먼저 들어가 보겠습니다 on your way out. Reality check: in actual Korean offices the honorific 수고하셨습니다 flies upward constantly and most bosses don't blink — the -시- softens it enough for daily use. But 'most' isn't 'all,' and older or more traditional seniors do register it. So: peers and juniors, use it freely; a boss, default to 감사합니다 and save 수고하셨습니다 for workplaces where you've heard others do it. The one form to genuinely avoid upward is present-tense 수고하세요 — it tells someone to keep laboring, which a junior is in no position to say. Against 고생하셨어요: 고생 leans on the hardship endured, so it's warmer and fits something genuinely grueling, while 수고하셨어요 is the routine end-of-task marker — but both carry the same upward caution. Against 감사합니다: that thanks them for a benefit to YOU and is safe in every direction, which is why it's the escape hatch.

structuredNuance.t: 수고하셨어요 credits the effort someone spent on a task — 'thanks for your hard work / good work.' It's an appraisal of their labor, not a thank-you for a favor done to you. That distinction is what drives all its register problems.

Direction matters more than the ending. Downward and sideways (juniors, peers, staff, delivery drivers) it's free and extremely common. Upward it's contested: 국립국어원's 표준 언어 예절 says not to use 수고하셨습니다 (or 고생하셨습니다) to 윗사람, because appraising a senior's effort is presumptuous — it recommends 감사합니다 / 고맙습니다 or 먼저 들어가 보겠습니다. In practice modern offices say 수고하셨습니다 upward all the time and most bosses don't mind; older or more traditional seniors still notice. Default to 감사합니다 with a boss until you've heard your colleagues do otherwise. Present-tense 수고하세요 ('keep working hard') is the one to genuinely avoid upward.

고생하셨어요 leans on the hardship endured — warmer, more sympathetic, right after something genuinely grueling (a move, an all-nighter, a long illness). 수고하셨어요 is the routine end-of-task marker. Both are appraisals of effort, so both carry the same upward caution — 고생하셨어요 is NOT the safe upward substitute people often assume it is. 감사합니다 thanks someone for a benefit to you and is safe in every direction; that's the real escape hatch.

수고했어 (casual, downward only) → 수고하셨어요 (polite) → 수고하셨습니다 (formal, meeting/workday close) → 수고 많으셨어요/많으셨습니다 (warmer, more deferential). Present tense 수고하세요 = 'keep it up,' said to someone still working as you leave.

Assuming the honorific -시- makes it safe upward — it fixes the verb, not the act of appraising a senior. Reaching for 고생하셨습니다 as the polite upward fix — same problem. Using it as a thank-you for a personal favor — it credits their labor but never says thanks, so you still need 감사합니다. And saying 수고하세요 to a professor or boss as you leave.

mistakes: Saying 수고하세요 to a boss or professor as you leave — the present tense means 'keep laboring,' an instruction a junior isn't in a position to give; say 먼저 들어가 보겠습니다 or 감사합니다.

Assuming 수고하셨습니다 is automatically safe upward because it has -시- in it — the honorific fixes the verb but not the act of appraising a senior's effort; 국립국어원 advises against it, real offices use it constantly, and traditional seniors still notice. Default to 감사합니다 with a boss.
Using 수고하셨어요 as your thank-you when someone did YOU a favor — it credits their effort but expresses no gratitude; add or switch to 감사합니다.

english: What a waste / so close — regret that something of real value got squandered or narrowly lost.
usage: what a waste / that's a pity
