polite -어요; -ㅂ irregular, so 아깝다 → 아까워요, never 아깝어요
casual banmal; also the reflex exclamation when someone just misses
casual exclamation half to yourself, softer and almost fond
examples: A: 남은 음식 그냥 버릴까요? / B: 아까워요. 싸 가면 안 돼요?
A: Should we just throw out the leftovers? / B: That's a waste. Can't we take them home?
textbook 아깝다 — something with real value is about to be discarded; 아쉬워요 would be wrong here
A: 1점 차로 졌어요 / B: 아, 아까워요. 거의 다 이겼는데.
A: We lost by one point / B: Ah, so close. You almost had it.
the near-miss use — the win was already in your hands and slipped away, so it feels squandered, not merely disappointing
A: 표 예매해 놓고 결국 못 갔어요 / B: 진짜 아까워요. 환불도 안 돼요?
A: I booked the ticket and then couldn't go / B: What a waste. Can't you get a refund?
money and an opportunity both went to nothing — 아깝다 is about the value lost, so the refund question follows naturally
nuance: 아깝다 is the feeling that something with real value went to nothing — money, food, time, effort, a chance you actually had — 'what a waste, that's too good to throw away.' Polite form is 아까워요 (-ㅂ irregular: 아깝 + 어요 → 아까워요), never 아깝어요. The distinction English speakers need most here is 아깝다 vs 아쉽다, because English flattens both into 'that's a shame.' 아깝다 needs an object of value that got wasted or lost: leftovers in the bin, a paid-for ticket unused, a match dropped by one point. 아쉽다 is about an expectation not met or something pleasant ending: the tickets sold out so you never had one, a friend is moving away, the trip was too short. The test: if you can point at what got squandered, it's 아깝다; if you're just wishing things had gone differently, it's 아쉽다. Sold-out concert → 아쉬워요 (you had no ticket to waste); a ticket you bought and couldn't use → 아까워요. One event can take both with different focus — after a narrow loss, 아까워요 says 'we had it and blew it' while 아쉬워요 says 'I'd hoped we'd win.' 아깝다 has a second life meaning 'too good for': 그 사람한테 네가 아까워 'you're too good for him,' and 시간이 아깝다 'that's a waste of time,' which is blunt. The pitfall is aiming 아깝다 at people or at grief.

structuredNuance.t: 아까워요 = 'what a waste / so close.' Something with real value — money, food, time, effort, a chance you actually held — went to nothing. There has to be a squandered THING behind it; the regret is about the value, not just the disappointment.

아까워요 is polite and safe with anyone you use 존댓말 with; 아깝다/아까워 is the banmal partner and also the reflex shout when someone just misses a shot. Conjugation trap: 아깝다 is a -ㅂ irregular adjective, so the polite form is 아까워요 (아깝+어요 → 아까워요), never 아깝어요.

아깝다 = value squandered or a near-miss you nearly had (leftovers binned, an unused ticket, a one-point loss). 아쉽다 = an expectation unmet or something pleasant ending (tickets sold out, a friend moving away, a short trip). Test: can you point at what got wasted? Then 아깝다. Sold-out concert → 아쉬워요; a ticket you bought and couldn't use → 아까워요. 안타깝다 = sympathetic distress at someone else's bad situation you can't fix — about them, not about wasted value.

아깝다 / 아까워 (casual) → 아까워요 (polite) → 아까워라 (soft exclamation to yourself) → 너무 아까워요 (intensified). Two fixed extensions worth knowing: 시간이 아깝다 'that's a waste of time' (blunt), and 그 사람한테 네가 아까워 'you're too good for him.'

Using 아까워요 for a sold-out show or a canceled plan — nothing of yours was wasted, so it's 아쉬워요. Conjugating 아깝어요 (-ㅂ irregular → 아까워요). Aiming it at a person you're parting from: 헤어지기 아까워요 sounds like you're calling them a squandered resource; it's 헤어지기 아쉬워요. And for a death, the emotion is 슬퍼요 / 안타까워요 — 아깝다 appears there only in the fixed 아까운 나이에 'cut down too young.'

mistakes: Using 아까워요 for something you never had — a sold-out concert or a canceled trip wasted nothing of yours, so it's 아쉬워요; 아까워요 needs value you actually held and lost.
Saying 헤어지기 아까워요 about a person you'll miss — 아깝다 frames them as a squandered resource; for missing someone the word is 아쉬워요 (헤어지기 아쉬워요).
Conjugating the -ㅂ irregular wrong as 아깝어요 — the polite form is 아까워요 (아깝+어요 → 아까워요), exactly parallel to 아쉽다 → 아쉬워요.
